## Introduction

<!-- OWNER: Stephanie (1-2 paragraphs) -->

<!-- Brief introduction to the dataset. You may repeat some of the information about the dataset provided in the introduction to the dataset on the TidyTuesday repository, paraphrasing on your own terms. Imagine that your project is a standalone document and the grader has no prior knowledge of the dataset. -->

This is the "Many Penguins" dataset, featured in TidyTuesday on 2026-07-14 (week 28), curated by Ben Bolker of McMaster University. It was created as a richer alternative to the Palmer Penguins dataset that includes only 3 species. Many Penguins dataset contains the penguins (Spheniscidae) records from the much larger AVONET database and includes 18 species.

We selected the Many Penguins dataset, derived from the global AVONET database (Tobias et al., 2022), because it lets us explore a question inspired by evolution: do closely related groups that share the same lifestyle end up with similar physical traits? The dataset includes 10 distinct morphometric measurements (physical body measurements) for 93 penguins from `r length(unique(penguins$species))` species within `r length(unique(penguins$genus))` genera. The dataset is cross-sectional and includes measurements of present-day penguin species, which provides a snapshot of penguins today rather than a record of their changes over time. Our goal is to describe and compare how beak shape and wing structure differ between the various penguin genera, and whether different genera remain physically distinct despite sharing an aquatic lifestyle.

```{r  data-overview}
# OWNER: Stephanie
# table: number of penguins and species per genus (sample sizes)
# table: number of F, M and U per genus (sex ratio)
# % missing per variable 

# Variables used in the analyses
analysis_vars <- c("beak.length_culmen", "beak.length_nares", "beak.width", "beak.depth", "tarsus.length", "hwi")

# Missing values in the beak measurements, by genus
missing_by_genus <- penguins %>%
  group_by(genus) %>%
  summarise(penguins = n(),
            # sum NAs per measurement variable
            across(all_of(analysis_vars), ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
            # sum all the unknown sex values
            sex_unknown = sum(sex == "U"))      
```

```{r tbl-missing}
                    "Beak width", "Beak depth", "Tarsus length", 
                    "Hand-wing index", "Unknown sex")) %>%
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) %>%
    kable_styling()
```

## Question 1: Do penguin genera differ in beak shape?

### Introduction

<!-- OWNER: Maria (1-2 paragraphs) -->

<!-- (1-2 paragraphs): Introduction to the question and what parts of the dataset are necessary to answer the question. Also discuss why you’re interested in this question.   -->

For this question we explore if penguins from the same genus have similar beak shapes that set them apart from other genera, and which part of the beak contributes most to these differences. The dataset includes four beak measurements: beak length (using two different measures), beak width, and beak depth. Together, they give a good picture of overall beak shape. We also use genus to group the penguins and tarsus length as a proxy for body size, so we can check whether differences in beak shape remain once size is removed. Moreover, since beak shape is closely related to diet and how an animal feeds, looking at these differences across genera may suggest how each group has adapted to find food in the ocean.

### Approach

<!-- OWNER: Maria (1-2 paragraphs) -->

<!-- (1-2 paragraphs): Describe what types of plots you are going to make to address your question. For each plot, provide a clear explanation as to why this plot (e.g. boxplot, barplot, histogram, etc.) is best for providing the information you are asking about. The two plots should be of different types, and at least one of the two plots needs to use either color mapping or facets. -->

<!-- - Figure 1: bar chart of PCA loadings, to show which beak measurement contributes most to each PC. -->

<!-- - Figure 2: PCA biplot (scatterplot of PC scores, coloured by genus, with loading arrows), faceted into original and size-corrected PCA. -->

<!-- Also to mention: log-transform and scale; complete cases or imputation; size correction using residuals on tarsus length. -->

We used Principal Component Analysis (PCA)[^1] on three beak measurements: culmen length, beak width and beak depth, using only penguins with all three measurements (complete cases; see @tbl-missing and the Analysis section for how we handled missing values). We log-transformed the measurements, which is standard for allometric data[^2] (Glazier, 2021), and scaled them so that no single measurement had too much weight. To check whether differences between genera were mainly due to size, we also ran the PCA on size-corrected data, using the residuals from regressing each log beak measurement on log tarsus length (a proxy for body size). Because the sign of a PC is arbitrary, we reversed PC1 and PC2 in the size-corrected PCA so that both analyses point in the same direction.

[^1]: PCA combines several related measurements into a few new axes, called principal components (PCs), which capture most of the variation in the data. This allows us to summarize the beak measurements in two-dimensional plots.

[^2]: Allometry refers to the way body parts change in proportion to overall body size; for example, larger penguins tend to have larger beaks. These relationships are usually curved on the original scale but become linear after a log transformation. Logging also makes differences between small and large penguins proportional.

The bar chart of the loadings (@fig-q1-loadings) shows how much each beak measurement contributes to each PC. A bar chart is well suited for this because the lengths of the bars can be compared along a common scale, which is easy to read accurately (Cleveland & McGill, 1984), so the measurement that drives each PC stands out. @fig-q1-biplot shows two PCA biplots, one above the other: the original PCA and the size-corrected PCA. Each biplot is a scatterplot of the PC scores of each penguin, with genera identified by a colour-blind-friendly palette and a different symbol, so they can be told apart without relying on color alone. Arrows are overlaid to show the loadings: each arrow points in the direction in which that beak measurement increases, so penguins located towards an arrow tend to have larger values of that measurement, and longer arrows indicate measurements that are better represented by the two PCs shown. Combined, the points and arrows show whether penguins of the same genus cluster and which measurements explain these clusters.

### Analysis

<!-- In this section, provide the code that generates your plots. Use scale functions to provide nice axis labels and guides. You are welcome to use theme functions to customize the appearance of your plot, but you are not required to do so. All plots must be made with {ggplot2}. Do not use base R or lattice plotting functions. -->

```{r q1-prepare}
# OWNER: Maria
# Numbers for inline code in the Approach
r_nares         <- cor(penguins$beak.length_culmen, penguins$beak.length_nares,
                       use = "complete.obs")
n_nares_missing <- sum(is.na(penguins$beak.length_nares))
n_depth_missing <- sum(is.na(penguins$beak.depth))

# Missing nares lengths and sample size for the two most affected genera
eudyptula <- missing_by_genus %>% filter(genus == "Eudyptula")
pygoscelis <- missing_by_genus %>% filter(genus == "Pygoscelis")

# keep penguins with all 3 beak measurements 
# Vector with the variable names of the four beak measurements 
pca_vars <- c("beak.length_culmen","beak.width", "beak.depth")

# Number of species

# Data frame for analyses: completecases and log transformation 
pca_dta <- penguins %>%
    # select variables for PCA analysis
    select(all_of(pca_vars), genus) %>%
    # just keep coplete cases
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    # log-transform the three beak measurements
    mutate(across(all_of(pca_vars), log, .names = "log_{.col}"))

# Vector with the log transformed variable names
pca_vars_log <- c("log_beak.length_culmen","log_beak.width", "log_beak.depth")
```

Before running the PCA, we explored missing values in the four beak measurements (@tbl-missing). While culmen length and beak width were complete, beak depth was missing for `r n_depth_missing` penguin, and nares length was missing for `r n_nares_missing` penguins, with the highest proportions in *Eudyptula* (`r eudyptula$beak.length_nares` of `r eudyptula$penguins`) and *Pygoscelis* (`r pygoscelis$beak.length_nares` of `r pygoscelis$penguins`). Because nares length was strongly correlated with culmen length (r = `r round(r_nares, 2)`), which also measures beak length, we excluded this measure to avoid losing these penguins. We considered imputing their values, but imputation would add little new information and could make genera appear more distinct than they are. Therefore, we ran the PCA on culmen length, beak width and beak depth, using only penguins with all three measurements (complete cases, n = `r nrow(pca_dta)`).

```{r q1-pca}
# OWNER: Maria (original PCA)
# PCA o the log transformed 3 measurements variables (not size-corrected)
pca_orig <- prcomp(pca_dta[,pca_vars_log], scale=T) 

# Percentage of variance explained by each PC
var_pc <- summary(pca_orig)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100

# Summary of the explained variance per component
summ_pca_var_nonsize <- summary(pca_orig)$importance

# Loadings of the PCs
summ_pca_load_nonsize <- pca_orig$rotation
```

```{r q1-pca-size}
# OWNER: Stephanie (size-corrected PCA)
# residuals of each log beak measurement on log(tarsus_length)
# Log-transform the beak measurements and tarsus length.
pca_size_dta <- penguins %>%
    select(all_of(pca_vars), tarsus.length, genus) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c(pca_vars, "tarsus.length")), log, .names = "log_{.col}"))

# Regress each log beak measurement on log tarsus length.
size_lm <- lm(as.matrix(pca_size_dta[, pca_vars_log]) ~ log_tarsus.length,
              data = pca_size_dta)

# Take the residuals: what's left of each beak measurement after removing 
# the part explained by body size.
beak_resid <- resid(size_lm)

# Run the PCA on the residuals.
pca_size <- prcomp(beak_resid, scale. = TRUE)

# Flip PC1 and PC2 signs (arbitrary in PCA) so panel B reads like panel A
pca_size$x[, 1:2]        <- -pca_size$x[, 1:2]
pca_size$rotation[, 1:2] <- -pca_size$rotation[, 1:2]

# Percentage of variance explained by each PC
var_pc_size <- summary(pca_size)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100

# Summary of the explained variance per component
summ_pca_var_size <- summary(pca_size)$importance

# Loadings of the PCs
summ_pca_load_size <- pca_size$rotation
```

For the size-corrected PCA, we used only penguins with all three beak measurements and tarsus length (n = `r nrow(pca_size_dta)`), compared with `r nrow(pca_dta)` penguins in the original PCA, because tarsus length is also missing for some individuals.

```{r tbl-q1-pca-variance}
# Table of variance explained by each PC 
kable(summ_pca_var_nonsize, digits = 2,
      caption = "Variance explained by each principal component 
      (PCA on log-transformed beak measurements, not size-corrected)") %>%
    kable_styling()
```

We observed that, together, PC1 and PC2 explained the `r round(summ_pca_var_nonsize[3,2]*100, 2)`% of the total varation (PC1: `r round(summ_pca_var_nonsize[2,1]*100, 2)`%; PC2: `r round(summ_pca_var_nonsize[2,2]*100, 2)`%). PC3 explained the remaining: `r round(summ_pca_var_nonsize[2,3]*100, 3)`% (@tbl-q1-pca-variance).

```{r q1-loadings-function}
# Loadings bar chart function: same design for the original and size-corrected PCA
make_loadings_plot <- function(pca, title) {
    # Percentage of variance explained by each PC
    var <- summary(pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100
    # Loadings of PC1 to PC3 in long format (one row per measurement and PC)
    loadings_long <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation[, c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3")]) %>%
        rownames_to_column("measurement") %>%
        mutate(measurement = c("Culmen length", "Beak width", "Beak depth")) %>%
        pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2, PC3), names_to = "PC", values_to = "loading") %>%
        mutate(PC = paste0(PC, " (", round(var[PC], 1), "%)"))
    
    # Bars of loadings: measurement on the y-axis, loading on the x-axis
    ggplot(loadings_long, aes(x = loading, y = measurement)) +
        # Grey vertical line at zero to separate positive and negative loadings
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        # One bar per measurement, in grey (colour is reserved for genus)
        geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.6) +
        # Loading value at the end of each bar
        geom_text(aes(label = round(loading, 2),
                      hjust = ifelse(loading < 0, 1.15, -0.15)),
                  size = 3.5, colour = "grey25") +
        # One panel per PC
        facet_wrap(~ PC) +
        # Same range for all panels, with room for the value labels
        scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.3, 1.3), breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5)) +
        labs(title = title, x = "Loading", y = NULL) +
        # Clean white theme with readable text size
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        # Light vertical gridlines only; bold panel and plot titles
        theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey93", linewidth = 0.3),
              strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))
}
```

```{r fig-q1-loadings}
#| fig-cap: "Loadings of the three log-transformed and scaled beak measurements on each principal component: (A) original PCA; (B) size-corrected PCA. Signs of PC1 and PC2 in (B) were reversed to match (A); signs in PCA are arbitrary."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
# OWNER: Maria

# Figure 1: bar charts of the PCA loadings
p_load_orig <- make_loadings_plot(pca_orig, "Original")
p_load_size <- make_loadings_plot(pca_size, "Size-corrected")

# One above the other, with panel tags A and B
p_load_orig / p_load_size + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

The loadings show that each principal component reflects a different dimension of the beak, and that this structure is almost the same before and after size correction (@fig-q1-loadings). In both PCAs, PC1 is dominated by beak width (original: `r round(summ_pca_load_nonsize["log_beak.width", "PC1"], 2)`; size-corrected: `r round(summ_pca_load_size["log_beak.width", "PC1"], 2)`) and beak depth (`r round(summ_pca_load_nonsize["log_beak.depth", "PC1"], 2)`; `r round(summ_pca_load_size["log_beak.depth", "PC1"], 2)`), so it represents how wide and deep (thick/robust) the beak is. PC2 is almost entirely determined by culmen length (`r round(summ_pca_load_nonsize["log_beak.length_culmen", "PC2"], 2)`; `r round(summ_pca_load_size["log_beak.length_culmen", "PC2"], 2)`) and therefore represents beak length, while PC3 contrasts beak width and depth, which load with opposite signs. The main difference is that culmen length contributes even less to PC1 after size correction (`r round(summ_pca_load_nonsize["log_beak.length_culmen", "PC1"], 2)` vs. `r round(summ_pca_load_size["log_beak.length_culmen", "PC1"], 2)`), so PC1 becomes an almost pure measure of beak thickness/robutness once size is removed. Together, PC1 and PC2 explain most of the variation in both PCAs (`r round(var_pc["PC1"] + var_pc["PC2"], 1)`% and `r round(var_pc_size["PC1"] + var_pc_size["PC2"], 1)`%), while PC3 explains little (`r round(var_pc["PC3"], 1)`% and `r round(var_pc_size["PC3"], 1)`%), so the biplots (@fig-q1-biplot) show only PC1 and PC2.

```{r q1-lda}
#| label: tbl-lda-cv
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-out cross-validated LDA classification of genus from log beak measurements (rows = actual, columns = predicted)"

# OWNER: Stephanie
# Linear discriminant analysis: how well can genus be predicted from the beak?

# use the same four log beak measurements (predictors) as the PCA, plus genus 
# (grouping variable to predict)
# MASS package does lda

# Leave-one-out cross-validation (CV = TRUE): each penguin is classified by a model fitted without that penguin, so the accuracy isn't over-optimistic
lda_cv <- MASS::lda(x = pca_dta[, pca_vars_log],
                    grouping = droplevels(pca_dta$genus),
                    CV = TRUE)

# table of actual vs predicted genus: table(actual, predicted) - no figure?, 
# we already will have two figures (PCA + loadings)
# % correct overall and per genus
actual <- droplevels(pca_dta$genus)
predicted <- lda_cv$class

#   Table of actual vs predicted genus (rows = actual, columns = predicted)
cm <- table(actual, predicted)

#   % correct overall
overall_pct <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm) * 100
       #equivalent: mean(predicted == actual) *100

#   % correct per genus (diagonal / row total, because rows = actual)
per_genus_pct <- diag(cm) / rowSums(cm) * 100

# make the table print with footnote of accuracy
cm_tbl <- cbind(as.data.frame.matrix(cm),
                `% correct` = per_genus_pct)
kable(cm_tbl, digits = 2) %>%
    kable_styling() %>%
    kableExtra::footnote(general = paste0("Overall accuracy: ", round(overall_pct, 1), "%"),
                         general_title = "")

```

```{r q1-biplot-function}
# Biplot function: same design for the original and size-corrected PCA
make_biplot <- function(pca, genus, labels, title, arrow_scale = 2.5) {
    # Percentage of variance explained by each PC
    var <- summary(pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100
    # PC1 and PC2 scores of each penguin, with its genus
    scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) |> mutate(genus = genus)
    # Loadings, stretched so the arrows are visible next to the points
    arrows <- as_tibble(pca$rotation[, 1:2] * arrow_scale) |>
        mutate(measurement = c("Culmen", "Width", "Depth"),
               # Mostly horizontal arrow (TRUE) or mostly vertical (FALSE)
               horiz = abs(PC1) >= abs(PC2),
               # Label just beyond the arrow tip
               lab_x = PC1 * 1.06,
               lab_y = PC2 * 1.06,
               # Horizontal: text starts at the tip and runs outwards;
               # vertical: text centred on the arrow
               hjust = ifelse(horiz, ifelse(PC1 < 0, 1, 0), 0.5),
               # Horizontal: the higher label is nudged up and the lower one down,
               # so labels of arrows pointing the same way do not overlap;
               # vertical: label above or below the tip
               vjust = ifelse(horiz,
                              ifelse(PC2 >= mean(PC2[horiz]), 0.2, 0.8),
                              ifelse(PC2 < 0, 1, 0)))

    ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
        # Grey lines at zero (centre of each PC)
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        # Penguins as points, coloured, shaped and sized by genus
        geom_point(aes(colour = genus, shape = genus, size = genus)) +
        # Arrows from the centre to each beak measurement's loading
        geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
                     arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")),
                     colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.7) +
        # Measurement names next to the arrow tips, with a white halo (no box);
        # force = 0 keeps them exactly where placed
        ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = arrows,
                                 aes(x = lab_x, y = lab_y, label = measurement,
                                     hjust = hjust, vjust = vjust),
                                 size = 3.5, colour = "grey25", fontface = "bold",
                                 bg.colour = "white", bg.r = 0.15,
                                 force = 0, force_pull = 0, segment.colour = NA,
                                 seed = 1) +
        # # Rounded white box with the genus name (right edge at label_x)
        # geom_label(data = labels,
        #            aes(x = label_x, y = label_y,
        #                label = paste0(genus, "     "), colour = genus),
        #            hjust = 1, fontface = "italic", size = 3.4, fill = "white",
        #            label.r = unit(0.5, "lines"),
        #            label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")) +
        # Genus symbol at the right end inside the box
        # geom_point(data = labels,
        #            aes(x = label_x - 0.17, y = label_y,
        #                colour = genus, shape = genus, size = genus)) +
        # Genus colours, shapes and sizes (same in every figure)
        scale_colour_manual(values = genus_cols) +
        scale_shape_manual(values = genus_shapes) +
        scale_size_manual(values = genus_sizes) +
        # Legend in two columns 
        guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
               shape  = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
               size   = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
        # Same limits in both panels so they have the same shape and align;
        # equal scale on both axes so distances are not distorted
        coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 2.5), clip = "off") +
        # Panel title and axis titles with % of variance
        labs(title = title,
             x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var["PC1"], 1), "%)"),
             y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var["PC2"], 1), "%)"),
             colour = "Genus", shape = "Genus", size = "Genus") +
        # Clean theme, light grid, no legend
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey93", linewidth = 0.3),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
              legend.title = element_blank(),
              legend.position = "inside",
              legend.position.inside = c(1.04, 0.02),
              legend.justification = c(1, 0),
              legend.text = element_text(face = "italic"),
              legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
              legend.margin = margin(4, 6, 4, 6))
}

```

```{r fig-q1-biplot}
#| fig-cap: "PCA biplots of beak shape across penguin genera: (A) log-transformed beak measurements; (B) after removing the effect of body size (residuals on log tarsus length). Each point is one penguin, coloured and shaped by genus; arrows show the loadings of the beak measurements. Percentages show the variance explained by each PC."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 10.5
# OWNER: Maria (figure), Stephanie (size-corrected PCA)

# Label positions (right edge of each box), original PCA
genus_labels <- tibble(
    genus   = c("Eudyptes", "Eudyptula", "Aptenodytes",
                "Spheniscus", "Pygoscelis", "Megadyptes"),
    label_x = c(-0.45, 3.85, 2.65, 2.6, 2.05, -0.55),
    label_y = c(1.8, 1.5, -2.6, 0.35, -0.85, -1.05)
)

# Label positions (right edge of each box), size-corrected PCA after flipping
genus_labels_size <- tibble(
    genus   = c("Eudyptes", "Eudyptula", "Aptenodytes",
                "Spheniscus", "Pygoscelis", "Megadyptes"),
    label_x = c(-2.0, 4.5, 3.0, 3.6, -1.2, 2.6),
    label_y = c(1.5, -0.7, -2.6, -1.9, -1.4, 2)
)

# The two biplots
p_orig <- make_biplot(pca_orig, pca_dta$genus, genus_labels, "Original", arrow_scale = 3.5)
p_size <- make_biplot(pca_size, pca_size_dta$genus, genus_labels_size, "Size-corrected", arrow_scale = 3.5)

# Side by side, with panel tags A and B
p_orig / p_size + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

**Original PCA.** Some genera form distinct groups in the biplot (@fig-q1-biplot). Aptenodytes separates along the culmen length arrow, indicating longer beaks, while Eudyptula lies opposite the width and depth arrows (narrower, shallower beaks). Eudyptes lies along width and depth arrows direction (wider, deeper beaks). Pygoscelis, Spheniscus and Megadyptes overlap in the centre. Because this PCA was not corrected for size, the extreme positions of the largest (Aptenodytes) and smallest (Eudyptula) penguins may partly reflect body size.

**Size-corrected PCA.** After removing the effect of body size, the same overall pattern remains, although the groups are less compact and overlap more (@fig-q1-biplot B). Aptenodytes still lies along the culmen length arrow, but closer to the centre, which suggests that its long beak is partly, but not only, explained by its large size. Eudyptula still lies opposite the width and depth arrows, so its beak remains relatively thin for its size, and Eudyptes still lies towards wider, deeper beaks. Pygoscelis, Spheniscus and Megadyptes continue to overlap in the centre. Overall, differences in beak shape between some genera persist once size is removed, so they are not simply a consequence of body size.

### Discussion

<!-- OWNER: Maria and Stephanie (Stephanie: size correction and LDA) -->

<!-- (1-3 paragraphs): In the Discussion section, interpret the results of your analysis. Identify any trends revealed (or not revealed) by the plots.Speculate about why the data looks the way it does. -->

<!-- What PC1 and PC2 represent; whether genera group together; which beak measurement contributes most; what changes after size correction; possible reasons (as interpretations); limitations. -->

Our PCAs showed that penguin beak variation is organised along two largely independent dimensions: beak thickness (width and depth, PC1) and beak length (PC2), which together explained `r round(summ_pca_var_nonsize[3,2]*100, 1)`% of the variation. Although we expected that PC1 would reflect overall beak size, culmen length contributed little to PC1. This means that penguins with thicker beaks do not necessarily have longer beaks. This suggests that beak length and thickness may have evolved somewhat independently across penguins, possibly in relation to different feeding demands, although our data cannot test this directly. Because we used only three beak measurements, a simple scatterplot of beak length against depth would show a similar pattern, but the PCA confirmed that width and depth vary together while length varies independently.

## Question 2: Does the hand-wing index still vary among penguin genera?

### Introduction

<!-- OWNER: Andrew (1-2 paragraphs) -->

<!-- I think the commented paragraph below could be merged into the general introduction at the beginning of the document, so it is a general description of the dataset. Here we can just focus on the introduction to this particular question. -->

<!-- This project uses the the "Many penguins" data set from the TidyTuesday project. The data is drawn from AVONET which is a global database that hold morphological, geographical, and ecological traits put together by Tobias et al. for basically all bird species. The data set that we are using is narrowed down to penguins, specially a group of `r length(unique(penguins$species))` living species in `r length(unique(penguins$genus))` different genera.  -->

The variable focused on in this question is the hand-wing index (named to hwi), which measures how elongated a penguins wing is. It is calculated as Kipp’s distance (the distance from the tip of the first secondary feather to the tip of the longest primary feather) divided by the total wing length, multiplied by 100. Ecologists commonly use it as a single-number proxy for flight efficiency and dispersal ability, with higher values indicating longer, more pointed wings (Sheard et al., 2020). Penguins are flightless and use their wings primarily as flippers. We are asking whether the trait tied to flight still differs between genera or has become similar across the group. If differences remain, they may reflect differences in flipper shape related to how each group swims and forages.

To answer the question, we compare the hand-wing index among the six penguin genera, and we use tarsus length as a proxy for body size to explore possible reasons for any differences.

<!-- OWNER: Andrew (1-2 paragraphs) -->

<!-- (1-2 paragraphs): Describe what types of plots you are going to make to address your question. For each plot, provide a clear explanation as to why this plot (e.g. boxplot, barplot, histogram, etc.) is best for providing the information you are asking about. The two plots should be of different types, and at least one of the two plots needs to use either color mapping or facets. -->

<!-- - Figure 3: boxplot of the hand-wing index by genus, with individual penguins as jittered points coloured by genus and the sample size (n) for each genus. -->

<!-- - Figure 4: mean hand-wing index per genus with 95% confidence intervals (point-and-interval plot), to judge whether genera are similar. -->

<!-- Also mention what test we chose, ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, and the effect size as support. -->

### Approach

To address our question we made two plots of different types. Figure 3 is a boxplot of the hand-wing index for each genus, with every penguin overlaid as a jittered point. Points are coloured and shaped by genus, and the sample size (n) is shown under each genus name on the x-axis. A boxplot is a good fit because it shows the median, spread and outliers of a numeric variable across several groups at once, which lets us compare the variability of each genus side by side. The jittered points keep the raw data visible, so genera with few penguins are not hidden behind a box, and colour makes each genus easy to follow. Figure 4 is a point-and-interval plot of the mean hand-wing index per genus with 95% confidence intervals. It answers a different question from Figure 3: instead of describing the spread of individual penguins, it shows how precisely each genus mean is estimated, so overlapping intervals suggest similar genera and clearly separated intervals suggest real differences. A bar chart would show the same means but not the uncertainty, so the interval plot is the better choice.

To check the visual impression, we test whether the hand-wing index differs among genera. Bartlett's test indicated unequal variances across genera (p = 0.038), so we use Welch's ANOVA, which does not assume equal variances, followed by Games-Howell pairwise comparisons to identify which genera differ. Since some genera have only four penguins, the low number of penguins can cause issues, so we also run a Kruskal-Wallis test as a robustness check and if both tests agree, our conclusion does not depend on the choice of test. As the effect size we report omega-squared, which is less biased than eta-squared for small groups and estimates the proportion of variation in hand-wing index explained by genus. Finally, because penguins of the same species are not independent observations, and Eudyptula and Megadyptes are each represented by a single species, we also summarise species level averages per genus in a table and compare them descriptively rather than testing them.

### Analysis

<!-- In this section, provide the code that generates your plots. Use scale functions to provide nice axis labels and guides. You are welcome to use theme functions to customize the appearance of your plot, but you are not required to do so. All plots must be made with {ggplot2}. Do not use base R or lattice plotting functions. -->

```{r q2-summary}
# OWNER: Andrew
# Filter out missing values
q2_data <- penguins |>
    filter(!is.na(hwi), !is.na(genus))

# summary per genus: n, mean, sd, median, 95% CI of the mean
q2_summary <- q2_data |>
    group_by(genus) |>
    summarise(
        n       = n(),
        mean    = mean(hwi),
        sd      = sd(hwi),
        median  = median(hwi),
        se      = sd / sqrt(n),
        ci_low  = mean - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
        ci_high = mean + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(mean))

q2_summary %>%
    mutate(ci = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", ci_low), " – ", sprintf("%.2f", ci_high))) %>%
    select(genus, n, mean, sd, median, ci) %>%
    kable(col.names = c("Genus", "n", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "95% CI"),
          digits = 2, align = c("l", rep("r", 5))) %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) %>%
    kable_styling() 
```

```{r q2-test}
# OWNER: Andrew
# Welch's ANOVA (main test), Games-Howell post hoc, omega-squared effect size,
# Kruskal-Wallis as a robustness check

# assumption checks (why Welch rather than standard ANOVA)
q2_data |>
    group_by(genus) |>
    filter(n() >= 3) |>
    summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(hwi)$p.value)

bartlett.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)

# main test: Welch's ANOVA (does not assume equal variances)
oneway.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data, var.equal = FALSE)

# post hoc: which genera differ
q2_gh <-rstatix::games_howell_test(q2_data, hwi ~ genus)

# effect size: omega-squared
fit <- aov(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)
ss  <- summary(fit)[[1]]
omega_sq <- (ss[1, "Sum Sq"] - ss[1, "Df"] * ss[2, "Mean Sq"]) /
    (sum(ss[, "Sum Sq"]) + ss[2, "Mean Sq"])
omega_sq

# robustness check: Kruskal-Wallis (no normality assumption)
kruskal.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)
```

```{r tbl-q2-posthoc}
#| tbl-cap: "Pairs of penguin genera whose mean hand-wing index differed significantly (Games-Howell test, adjusted p < 0.05). Difference = mean of the genus with the higher index minus the mean of the genus with the lower index, with its 95% confidence interval. All other pairs did not differ significantly."
# OWNER: Andrew
# Significant pairwise comparisons, with the higher-index genus listed first

q2_gh |>
    filter(p.adj < 0.05) |>
    # Swap genera when the difference is negative, so all differences are positive
    mutate(higher  = if_else(estimate > 0, group2, group1),
           lower   = if_else(estimate > 0, group1, group2),
           diff    = abs(estimate),
           ci_low  = if_else(estimate > 0, conf.low, -conf.high),
           ci_high = if_else(estimate > 0, conf.high, -conf.low),
           ci      = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", ci_low), " – ", sprintf("%.2f", ci_high)),
           p_adj   = format.pval(p.adj, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    arrange(desc(diff)) |>
    select(higher, lower, diff, ci, p_adj) |>
    kable(col.names = c("Higher index", "Lower index", "Difference", "95% CI", "Adjusted p"),
          digits = 2, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
    column_spec(1:2, italic = TRUE)
```

```{r fig-q2-boxplot}
#| fig-cap: "caption for Figure 3"
# OWNER: Andrew
# geom_boxplot + geom_jitter, colour and shape = genus, n per genus

q2_labelled <- q2_data |>
    add_count(genus, name = "n") |>
    mutate(genus_n = fct_reorder(paste0(genus, "\n(n = ", n, ")"),
                                 hwi, .fun = median))

ggplot(q2_labelled, aes(x = genus_n, y = hwi)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = NA, colour = "darkgrey", width = 0.5) +

    scale_y_continuous(name = "Hand-wing index") +
    scale_x_discrete(name = "Genus (sample size)") +
    
    ### MARI comment: I added the defined palettes on top of teh document to be consistent with colors and shapes through the document
    scale_colour_manual(values = genus_cols, guide = "none") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = genus_shapes, guide = "none") +
    scale_size_manual(values = genus_sizes, guide = "none") +
    # scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +

    #                    guide = "none") +
    theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-q2-ci}
#| fig-cap: "caption for Figure "
# OWNER: Andrew
# geom_pointrange (mean and 95% CI per genus)
# Penguins with both a hand-wing index and a tarsus length
q2_size <- q2_data |>
    filter(!is.na(hwi), !is.na(tarsus.length))

# Centre (median) of each genus and its sample size, for the genus names
# Penguins with both a hand-wing index and a tarsus length
q2_size <- q2_data |>
    filter(!is.na(hwi), !is.na(tarsus.length))

q2_size_labels <- q2_size |>
    group_by(genus) |>
    summarise(n = n(),
              tarsus.length = median(tarsus.length),
              hwi = median(hwi))

ggplot(q2_size, aes(x = tarsus.length, y = hwi)) +
    # Individual penguins, coloured, shaped and sized by genus
    geom_point(aes(colour = genus, shape = genus, size = genus), alpha = 0.85) +
    # Genus names near the centre of each genus, moved apart if they overlap
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = q2_size_labels,
                             aes(label = genus, colour = genus),
                             fontface = 'italic', size = 4,
                             bg.colour = 'white', bg.r = 0.15,
                             box.padding = 0.8, min.segment.length = Inf,
                             seed = 1) +
    # Axis titles
    scale_x_continuous(name = "Tarsus length (mm)") +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Hand-wing index") +
    # Genus colours, shapes and sizes (same in every figure); no legend
    scale_colour_manual(values = genus_cols, guide = "none") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = genus_shapes, guide = "none") +
    scale_size_manual(values = genus_sizes, guide = "none") +
    # Clean theme with light gridlines
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r q2-explore}
# OWNER: Stephanie
# Exploratory checks for possible reasons why the hand-wing index varies (no figures)
# 1. body size: Spearman correlation between hwi and tarsus_length
size_cor <- cor.test(q2_data$hwi, q2_data$tarsus.length,
                     method = "spearman", exact = FALSE) 
# exact = FALSE because tied values prevent an exact p-value
size_cor

# 2. components of the index: mean kipps_distance and wing_length per genus
q2_components <- q2_data |>
  group_by(genus) |>
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    mean_kipps  = mean(kipps.distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_wing   = mean(wing.length, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hwi    = mean(hwi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # ratio of the two means: a quick check that it tracks mean hwi
  mutate(kipps_wing_ratio = 100 * mean_kipps / mean_wing) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_hwi))

#    (small table), to see which part drives any differences
# 3. sex: refer to the sex-ratio table from the Introduction; note any genus
#    dominated by one sex
q2_sex <- q2_data |>
  group_by(genus) |>
  summarise(
    F_n = sum(sex == "F", na.rm = TRUE),
    M_n = sum(sex == "M", na.rm = TRUE),
    U_n = sum(sex == "U", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # % male among penguins of known sex
    pct_male = 100 * M_n / (F_n + M_n),
    dominated = case_when(pct_male >= 70 ~ "mostly male",
                          pct_male <= 30 ~ "mostly female",
                          TRUE ~ "balanced")
  )

# This table shows comparing mean Kipp’s distance and wing length across genera to therefore see which part of the hand-wing index drives any differences between them.
#| tbl-cap: "Mean Kipp's distance, wing length and hand-wing index by genus"
kable(
    q2_components,
    col.names = c("Genus", "Penguins", "Mean Kipp's distance",
                  "Mean wing length", "Mean hand-wing index",
                  "100 × Kipp's / wing"),
    digits = 1,
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE)
```
